newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM's spouse lifts lid on first wives' talk.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM's spouse lifts lid on first wives' talk.

text.p: The wife of Japan's prime minister has given a rare glimpse into what first ladies talk about when they meet, revealing she discussed dog droppings with Bernadette Chirac and elderly women giving birth with Hillary Clinton.
In a magazine interview, Kumiko Hashimoto also gave a behind-the-scenes look at how home life has changed since her husband Ryutaro became Japan's prime minister 18 months ago.

Her revelations include disclosures that Hashimoto gets home earlier now he is prime minister, has taken to drinking liquor at home with his meals, is an avid comic reader and that she doesn't like his trademark, slicked back hair.

Kumiko Hashimoto's candid interview published this week in the latest issue of the influential monthly magazine Bungei Shunju marked a radical change from past tradition of Japanese first ladies being seen but rarely heard.
Mrs Hashimoto said she found first wives around the world tried "to avoid talking about anything too complex" when they met.
"As a result, we end up talking about things that normal middle-aged housewives talk about," she said.
Recalling a meeting last April at the White House with Hillary Clinton, Mrs Hashimoto said the pair talked about women who gave birth late in life.

"She probably thought of a conversation that would suit me, but we spoke about a lady who is in the Guinness Book of Records for giving birth at 63 years of age. I wondered if that was a conversation to hold with the first lady in the White House."
Mrs Hashimoto's conversation with French President Jacques Chirac's wife, Bernadette, in Paris took a different turn.
"When I met Mrs Chirac for a meal we ended up talking about walking our dogs and Mrs Chirac said Paris is full of dog droppings and asked me what we do about the problem in Japan."
Mrs Hashimoto, a 55-year-old mother of five who beats her husband, 59, at golf, does not find a problem in finding topics for conversation when she and her husband are at home together.

"I'm like a garbage can," she said. "When he wants to talk about events, I listen, although I don't ask him questions. I tend to forget everything on first hearing them from my husband so I'm like a garbage can."

Reflecting on how home life had changed, Mrs Hashimoto said the couple woke 30 minutes earlier than when her husband was simply a cabinet minister holding high profile posts such as finance and trade minister. But the prime minister now ended the day earlier at around 7 p.m.
"You might think this is strange, but my husband has been coming home early since he became prime minister," she said.
"When he was trade minister, he had dinner meetings almost every day and so he had dinner at home maybe once a week, if at all. That's why he never drank at home, for a 'liver holiday'," she said.

"The big change since becoming prime minister is he drinks at the dinner table now. But it's not that much. He takes maybe one or two small bottles of cold sake, or maybe hot whiskey when we have Western food."
Mrs Hashimoto said her spouse transformed from husband to prime minister during the 30 minutes he took to do his hair.

"I don't think much of his hairstyle and everybody makes an issue out of it so I have begun to think it could be abnormal," she said. "I like natural hair, but I'd only tell him that if he asked for my opinion."
Mrs Hashimoto said despite demands on her husband's time, he still managed to read their children's comic books.
"He reads them all, then he reads them again," she said.
